lesson.title: The Rulebook for Particles in Motion
lesson.summary: Kinetic molecular theory is a small set of assumptions about how gas particles move and collide, and it is what connects the everyday behavior of gases to the more general picture of states of matter driven by particle energy.
lesson.body:
Kinetic molecular theory is a model built from a handful of assumptions about how the particles of a gas behave, and it gives a physical explanation for why gases act the way they do rather than just describing that behavior with equations. The theory was developed primarily to explain ideal gases, but its core idea, connecting particle motion and energy to observable bulk behavior, is the same idea used to explain the states of matter more broadly.

The theory rests on five main postulates. First, a gas consists of a huge number of particles in constant, random, straight-line motion, changing direction only when they collide with something. Second, the volume of the individual gas particles themselves is assumed to be negligible compared to the total volume of the container they occupy, so gas particles are treated essentially as points. Third, gas particles are assumed to exert no attractive or repulsive forces on one another between collisions, meaning intermolecular forces are ignored entirely in the ideal case. Fourth, collisions between gas particles, and between particles and the container walls, are perfectly elastic, meaning no kinetic energy is lost overall during a collision, even though individual particles can speed up or slow down. Fifth, the average kinetic energy of the particles is directly proportional to the absolute temperature of the gas, measured in Kelvin, and this average kinetic energy is the same for any gas at a given temperature regardless of the identity of the particles.

That last postulate is where kinetic molecular theory connects back most directly to energy and to the broader picture of states of matter. Because average kinetic energy depends only on temperature, raising the temperature of a gas increases how fast its particles move on average, which in turn increases how forcefully and how often they collide with the container walls, producing higher pressure if volume is held constant, or increasing volume if pressure is held constant. This is the particle-level explanation behind the pressure, volume, and temperature relationships you see in gas laws.

Real gases deviate from this idealized model, and the deviations are informative rather than just being errors to correct. The assumption of negligible particle volume breaks down at high pressure, when particles are squeezed close enough together that their actual size starts to matter. The assumption of no intermolecular forces breaks down at low temperature, when particles are moving slowly enough that even weak attractions, like dispersion forces or dipole-dipole forces, become significant enough to pull particles together, which is part of what eventually causes a gas to condense into a liquid as it cools. Gases made of larger, more polarizable molecules, or polar molecules, deviate from ideal behavior more than small nonpolar gases like helium, precisely because those larger or polar molecules experience stronger intermolecular forces that the ideal model assumes away. Seen this way, kinetic molecular theory is not just a rule set for gases in isolation, but the same competition between particle motion and intermolecular attraction that determines whether a substance is a solid, liquid, or gas in the first place.
